title: Team Members Who Are Afraid of Disagreement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines why some team members shy away from disagreement — often out of fear of being judged, appearing uninformed, or damaging relationships — and offers a coaching approach for leaders to help them build tolerance for dissent. The recommended method starts small: practicing disagreement on low-stakes, inconsequential topics to build confidence before extending the practice to substantive team discussions. Leaders are advised to give reticent team members advance notice that their opinion will be solicited, to press for more detail when they simply agree with the group, and to thank them for contributing even uncomfortable views. The article frames this as essential coaching work because teams cannot make good decisions without candid participation from everyone.
points: Some team members avoid disagreement out of fear of judgment, rejection, or damaged relationships rather than a lack of opinions.
Leaders can build their tolerance for dissent by first practicing disagreement on inconsequential, low-stakes topics.
Giving advance warning before calling on a reticent team member, and thanking them for engaging, reinforces the behavior over time.
Teams cannot reach quality decisions without candid participation, so coaching disagreement-averse members is a leadership responsibility.
quotes: Although it is sometimes hard for leaders to fully grasp, some team members are simply afraid of disagreement.
Consider that some team members fear disagreement because they are afraid of being judged or rejected.
A belief that disagreement may weaken bonds and harm relationships can serve as a major impediment.
Playful arguing over favorite shows, service providers, music preferences, and current news events provides these team members with the necessary practice
Without disagreement, people and teams don’t make progress. Learning that can be a life-changer for those frightened by debate.
